utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and to those who are following our procedures. Mr. McCloskey, are you in a position to update us about the matters we discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, everyone. Yes, I would like to be able to announce that today we will file 92 quater motions for Witness 192 and Witness 193 and that for witnesses 61, 42, 94, and 95 we will be -- are asking that they be withdrawn. And I can file something or just do this orally, however you'd wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Is the Defence in a position to indicate when they will be able to respond? Taking into account the short time of the remainder of the Prosecution case, we would be happy if the Defence would be able to respond as soon as possible. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence will respond as soon as we are physically able to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Whatever that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that we will do everything in our power to respond as soon as possible. First, we have to review 92 quater requests and will respond shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then in that case we will wait for the motion the Prosecution pursuant to 92 quater in relation to two witnesses. Can I take it that the four witnesses are now withdrawn by your oral submission, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no other matters, we should -- the witness should be brought in, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, you should all have our list of the remaining witnesses and our estimated times, and I've spoken to Mr. Gajic about that. And we hope to be able to work roughly within those times. Witness Pecanac may be hard to gauge the time that he will take, but the rest don't appear to be very time consuming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, Mr. Butler. Welcome back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace in this house and may God's will be done in these proceedings today and not mine. Greetings to everyone present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Butler, too. Mr. Butler, yesterday we discussed the conversation with Mr. Mladic and the threat that sanctions would be imposed if UNPROFOR convoys were subject of attack? This is something that we discussed. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember we had discussions related to this within the context of General Smith's witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's correct. I'll read the relevant sentence. Smith said that he spoke to Karadzic on the 9th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate where we can find it in the statement of Mr. Smith so that we can have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, my apologies, Mr. President. We will find the relevant portion of General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show D193, page 13, paragraph 2. That's page 12, penultimate or last paragraph of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You mean page 12 in the English; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. The last paragraph, which reads: "On the 9th May, I had a further private meeting with Dr. Karadzic. The discussions covered the recent BSA attacks on Sarajevo and the Bosnian Serb sanctions on the UN contingents in the eastern enclaves." Can we now show 65 ter 724. 7248, my apologies. Thank you, Aleksandar. This is another report about the interview that the OTP had with General Rupert Smith on the 8th of November, 2011. Can we have page 4 displayed in both versions, paragraphs 1 through 3. It seems that we are looking after paragraph 5, after all. Let me quote: "I predicted under the thesis that the Serbs would neutralise those enclaves to eliminate the need to place BSA forces. "Then there was the routine denial of convoys. There was the shooting down of two Bosnian helicopters flying one into Gorazde and into Srebrenica. "I thought to myself, what if I was Mladic? What would I do to shift the balance of forces to advantage of the Serbs? I would squeeze the enclaves, make them irrelevant, starve them."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: In this particular quotation, did General Rupert Smith present his view as to what he would have done had he been in the shoes of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular -- this second statement which I believe you're incorrect, it's not dated 2011, I believe it's dated 2002. I am not sure if I've ever read it before, so I don't know the entire context of the statement, but from the passage that you laid out, General Smith is theorising that if he were General Mladic, how he would approach the situation with respect to shifting, again, that balance of power and not necessarily strength but the ability to free up forces to use them in other parts of the country. That shifting, that balance of been -- of forces to the advantage of the Serbs, how he would do it. In his case, he's basically saying that he would deal with the situation in the eastern enclaves. He recognised, as General Mladic did, that they were an intolerable strain on the man power resources of the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. General Smith goes on to say further down: "I would squeeze the enclaves, make them irrelevant, starve them." Was this, too, a view that he expressed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- in the context of his witness statement, it's probably not the most artful phrase that he might have used in describing the situation, but what it says is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. If these eastern enclaves, which were deep within the territory of Republika Srpska, and if they attacked the territory of the Republika Srpska, is not the Army of Republika Srpska entitled to use measures against them including UNPROFOR forces which failed to enforce the demilitarisation to which measures they would be entitled under the legal provisions arising from the Geneva Conventions that we looked at yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've indicated before, I've always believed that the VRS had the right to attack the elements of the 28th Infantry Division in both the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. Those represented legitimate military targets. As for the second part of your question, whether or not they were entitled to use measures against the United Nations protection forces is a thornier question. For good or for bad, the United Nations protection forces did not see themselves as a party to the conflict. I understand that from the Bosnian Serb military perspective, they were viewed as, at least tacitly, aiding the Bosnian Muslim forces in the enclaves, or the enclaves with respect to the eastern enclaves. So, again, there was never any problem conducting military operations against the 28th Infantry Division. They represented a legitimate military target as such. I am always problematic with respect to whether or not anyone is entitled to attack the United Nations forces under those same scenarios.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. A moment ago you said that they aided the Muslim forces, and I mean UNPROFOR. Are not the Bosnian Serbs entitled to restrict the aid arriving for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially if the aid happens to be transiting the territory under their control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said specifically was that I understand that from a military perspective the Bosnian Serb side viewed that UNPROFOR was aiding the Bosnian Muslim side. I have no first-hand knowledge whether they were or were no it. As to the second part of your question, the Bosnian Serb side obviously did have the view that since they believed that the UNPROFOR was aiding the Bosnian Muslim side, that by restricting supplies going into the United Nations or for United Nations forces, that that would have a follow-on effect and militarily impact or degradate the ability of the Bosnian Muslim military forces to conduct further operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Yesterday and this morning we've been discussing the mandate of the United Nations forces, specifically the Dutch Battalion in the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up D20. It's a report based on the debriefing which was published in 1995. We are interested in page 9, paragraph 23 -- 223, which describes the mandate of the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica. This is the title: "Debriefing." Can we have page 9, paragraph 2.23. Can we have the next page, please. Thank you. We see there 2.23. You can see it. We are discussing the mandate of the Dutch Battalion as expressed here: "The tasks assigned to DutchBat were as follows, derived from the aforementioned cease-fire and resolutions." Under A: "To monitor compliance with the cease-fire. "B. To disarm the BiH. "C. To support the provision of humanitarian aid."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Based on your knowledge and reading of the relevant documents including perhaps this debriefing, is what I just read out the basis for the mandate of the DutchBat that was present in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this particular document and laying this situation out, these were the three provisions that came out of the 1995 report, so this is what initially that they understood their mission to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, was any of these tasks completed by the UNPROFOR forces stationed in Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the three tasks, I believe that task A, monitoring the compliance, and task C, were tasks that were always going to be ongoing, and the Dutch Battalion took measures to do that. I do not believe that by the time we got to the third iteration of Dutch Battalion, DutchBat III, that they were actively involved in task B anymore, which was disarming the BiH forces within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at D239 now. It's a report from the sector of intelligence and security of the Main Staff of VRS, dated the 19th of May, 1995. Can we show page 2, please, in Serbian, and page 3 in English. We have it now. Thank you. The relevant part reads: "We have confirmed the information that the 28th Division is undergoing intensive preparations for offensive activities in order to link up with elements of the 23rd Division in the Han Pogled area. As part of offensive preparations from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, they have taken possession of important features to secure the corridor linking the enclaves, and they have partially grouped the forces in the western part of the enclaves. They have taken Podravanje, Ljeskovik, Susica, Stublic, Brloznik, Sadilov Cair, Godjenje, Ljubomislje, and Gusinac, which are outside of the so-called demilitarised zone, which is also to create better conditions for offensive activities." So this is document dated 19th May, 1995, which is two months ahead of the VRS operations directed at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, should UNPROFOR know that they are leaving the demilitarised zone and taking up positions, as indicated here, which were part of the operation of linking up?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you are aware, the UN Dutch Battalion forces did have a number of observation posts around the perimeter of the enclave, along not necessarily the demarcated border because the demarcated border was disputed. I would again remind you that whether they should have known or should not have known, the reality was that once restrictions of movements were put into place by the BiH 28th Infantry Division in March of 1995, and perhaps even as early as February, the actual ability of the Dutch Battalion to monitor all of these types of operations would have been greatly degraded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. You're probably thinking of this particular document of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show D142, please. Thank you. We have the document in Serbian and we'll shortly have it in English, I suppose. We are interested in paragraph 3, to summarise what you discussed, and I'm quoting: "The Corps command must agree with the UNPROFOR liaison officer stationed there on the procedure when giving advance notice to the commands of the brigades, battalions, and lines of defence of the BH Army of movement and checks by groups, teams, patrols, and others from the UNPROFOR contingent. UNPROFOR movement has to be channelled and reduced as much as possible in places where they can observe and gather intelligence."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the command of the BH Army of the Corps in Tuzla, sent on the 4th of January, 1995, to Srebrenica. You are right on that score. However, this is my question: Because of all this, was UNPROFOR under the supervision of the BH Army in Srebrenica or was it the other way around? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure I can claim that the UNPROFOR was under the supervision of the BH Army in Srebrenica, but, again, I certainly concede what I've always said on this same issue which is that one these restrictions on movement went into place, the ability of the Dutch Battalion to effectively monitor ABiH military movements and activities within the enclave were greatly restricted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Was it the case then that the Army of Republika Srpska which had its territory in the area where the enclaves are situated, aren't they entitled, in fact, to make sure that UNPROFOR does what it was supposed to do; i.e., disarm the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that is a constant theme within the reporting of the VRS, and particularly the Drina Corps, which is the fact that they do not believe that the UN forces were living up to what they believe was the mandate, and part of that mandate, under the cease-fire agreements, was to disarm the Bosnian Muslim forces or to ensure that they remained disarmed within the enclave. The Dutch Battalion and the UN forces, for their reasons, elected not to force the issue with 1st Operations Group 8 and later the 28th Infantry Division. They allowed that status quo to remain, and, as a result, that status quo permitted the 28th Infantry Division to conduct operations out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean, Mr. Butler, that UNPROFOR forces deployed in Srebrenica failed to fulfill their mandate with regard to the parties to the conflict and that they favoured one of the sides and, in fact, allowed it to organise itself militarily?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether or not they failed to fulfill their mandate again revolves around the question of what the United Nations from top to bottom believed their mandate was with respect to the safe areas. As you can tell even from this document that you have here, from the 2nd Corps command, even the Bosnian Muslim military forces believed that the UNPROFOR forces in the Srebrenica enclave were, in fact, gathering information related to their military operations to their detriment. Both sides perceived that the United Nations forces were not acting impartially within the enclave. The Bosnian Serb side had their position which was that the UNPROFOR was tacitly aiding the Bosnian Muslim military forces: One, overtly by not disarming them; and, two, through the convoy activities and humanitarian resupply which they believed was being siphoned to some degree to support the 28th Infantry Division. The Bosnian Muslims on their side, particularly as you get closer to July of 1995, actually go as far as believing that the United Nations mandate for the safe area should be defined as defending the safe area from the attack by the Bosnian Serb military forces. So in this particular context, the United Nations protection forces were viewed very badly by both sides with respect to what they were supposed to be doing within the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Please, can you tell me this: If UNPROFOR forces in the enclaves had the mandate to disarm the BH, did they also have the mandate to collect intelligence data about the developments in the enclaves with respect to the procedure of arming, and were they entitled to confiscate such weaponry and put them in a safe depot because according to the agreement, even paramilitary formations were subject to disarming in the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dealing first with your question on intelligence information, I would suspect that while the UN would never qualify it as collecting intelligence on warring parties, the reality will be that the UN commanders on the ground are going to want to keep and be informed as much as possible about what is happening in the enclave, if for no other reason than to assure the protection and security of the UN forces. So there will be intelligence collection or reconnaissance activities going on by the UN. With respect to the collection of weapons, the UN DutchBat forces there did, in fact, collect weapons, particularly early on in 1993, and they were monitored. The problem that was ongoing was that the United Nations would only monitor the weapons that were turned in by the Bosnian Muslim military side. They would not actively go out and seek to disarm those particular units. So on the one hand, they guarded whatever material that was turned over to them, much of it, as it turns out, was either inoperative or obsolete; but on the other hand, they did not do anything with respect to actively going out and confiscating military equipment or supplies that they might have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. If their main task was to effect the disarming of all forces in the enclave, why were they then concealing their task with regard to gathering intelligence about both the regular military and paramilitary forces inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe they were concealing it as such. All parties knew that the United Nations forces, as part of the monitoring the enclave, were going to go out and conduct reconnaissance operations. In fact, when you go back to this document that you have on the screen with respect to the 2nd Corps command, it is precisely because of the fact that the ABiH military forces are aware that the Dutch are doing this that they seek to restrict their movement so they can prevent the Dutch from gaining information on these military units and other such information that they deemed would be vital to keep from the Dutch. So it's not a secret that they are doing it. What I'm trying to get the point across is that I would suspect that the UN would not ever claim that they are actually conducting intelligence operations. I mean, they are to be a neutral party. And in this particular context, I don't believe, you know, doing reconnaissance of an area that they are supposedly protecting or monitoring is going to qualify as intelligence gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, did you ever read any kind of document containing information about the relationships between UNPROFOR and the commands of staffs and the 28th Division or any other unit because this is mentioned in this document? Was it allowed for a demilitarised side to have liaison officers to communicate with UNPROFOR in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware from the various documents that I've read with respect to Srebrenica, that both sides, not only the Bosnian Muslim side but the Bosnian Serb military side, had protocols in place and officers who were designated to be liaison officers, not only with the Dutch Battalion but with the independent United Nations military observers within Srebrenica. So there was, at least, a mechanism by which not only the UN observers but the Dutch Battalion officers could contact both their counterparts within the VRS as well as their counterparts within the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were units such as battalion and brigades supposed to exist in Srebrenica, and if the proper demilitarisation had been conducted, would the situation have been any different?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to your first question, I suppose in the abstract that the 2nd Corps could have decided to keep a military organisational structure for Operations Group 8 and later the 28th Infantry Division and still had them completely disarmed in full compliance with the agreement. I don't know that that would have made much sense to do but they could have done it. The second question, I am not sure that I can answer. It requires a bit of speculation on my part. I don't know whether or not it's known or can be known if -- had the 28th Division been completely disarmed, whether or not history would have happened the way that it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Given that UNPROFOR maintained legal contact with a military organisation structure in a demilitarised zone, have you come across any documents confirming that they provided them with humanitarian aid even though they were dealing with a military organisation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any document specifically from the Dutch component of the United Nations which reflects that UN supplies to the Dutch Battalion were being siphoned off or provided to the ABiH. I am aware that various civilian organisations within the enclave, at times, did make complaints to the Dutch that various other humanitarian goods that were brought in under other UN or international auspices were stolen, siphoned off for military use, or being sold on the black market. So I guess I differentiate between those supplies that are going directly to -- and are manifested to the Dutch Battalion for their use versus a broader pool of supplies that were going in to provide support for the larger civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have in e-court D80. In the meantime, I would like to tender into evidence D142.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, the last document, D142 was marked for identification pending future identification. It will now be received as D142 as a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have D80 in e-court. Thank you. This is a document produced by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Federation of BH, and their defence ministry, specifically their defence secretariat of Tuzla, Srebrenica department, submitted on the 5th of June, 1995, to the Tuzla defence secretariat in which they are reporting about the situation and aid arriving in Srebrenica. And it says: "We hereby submit a list of the quantities of food, materiel, and technical equipment and fuel issued to our military units in our area from the month of May 1995." Then it says: "25.900 kilogrammes of flour, 596 kilogrammes of sugar, 1.423 litres of cooking oil, 619 kilogrammes of salt, 5.000 kilogrammes of beans, 17.020 of cold cuts, 100 kilogrammes of powder milk, 62 kilogrammes of juice, 7.000 [as interpreted] of tins." Then it speaks about, "Carrot, beans, 171 litres of fuel, engine oil, 1 litre. "We wish to note that the above quantities have been separated from the humanitarian aid contingent which arrived in the area through the UNHCR, while some of the food was obtained from the Dutch Battalion. "Till our ultimate victory! "Chief of the Defence sector, Professor Suljo Hasanovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Can one infer from this document that the Dutch Battalion was providing assistance to the Army of Bosnian-Herzegovina as well in the Srebrenica enclave consisting of food supplies, fuel, and other necessities and items listed here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the context of this document it certainly does claim that they obtained some of the food from the Dutch Battalion. It doesn't specify that they obtained fuel or other such items. And I guess the question that I would have before agreeing to a statement like that, is whether or not the Dutch would ultimately have been aware that the food that they were supplying was actually going to the military versus to civilian needs. So while I accept the fact from this particular document that the 28th Infantry Division and the military forces within Srebrenica are getting food from these sources, one of which is the Dutch Battalion, the question that I would have is whether or not the Dutch Battalion personnel were aware that they were supplying food for the ABiH army as opposed to providing food for civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One short remark, on my part. You have read into the transcript the content of this document, Mr. Tolimir, in relation to the 171 litres. You said -- or I heard in the interpretation the word "fuel." In the English translation I see "heating oil" in relation to 171 litre. It may be a translation issue. I don't know. Just for the record. Please -- Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, obviously there is a slight mistake in the translation because in the original it says "oil," "171 litres of oil."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see the word "nafta." Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order not to dwell on these issues any longer since we see that there were no activities leading to the disarming, and you said that yourself. Now let us look at task C. That is to say, did they provide support in providing humanitarian aid? In other words, can you tell me whether UNPROFOR provided support in providing humanitarian aid and did they, themselves, provide humanitarian supplies? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR, within the context of the Srebrenica enclave, one, their primary mission was to resupply their own United Nations forces; the second one was to facilitate the movement of supplies by other United Nations or international agencies to the enclaves for the general population. It was not the UNPROFOR's job per se to supply the civilian population within the enclave. It was the UNPROFOR's job to provide security, to monitor the enclave, and create the conditions where other United Nations and international agencies would do that. So I mean, I guess it's a bit of an artificial distinction, but from the United Nations' perspective it's probably an important one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please, since you spoke about the role of UNPROFOR in delivering the relief, under the Geneva Conventions did UNPROFOR have any right to check and control the ultimate destination relief and to whom it was distributed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question. I am not sure of how -- in enough detail how the process would have worked with respect to what UN -- UN protection force procedures were in place to verify that aid coming in from other United Nations agencies or other international organisations were given strictly to civilians or noncombatants and did not make their way to combatant forces. I just don't know enough about how that process worked and what the protocols were to be able to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, were they entitled then to monitor or supervise the distribution of this humanitarian aid to prevent it to going to the places where it is not intended to go, such as smuggling channels, black markets, and things of that sort?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I don't know if that was a specific mission mandate of the United Nations protection forces or whether that remained a task that the actual agencies providing the aid would be responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, do you know what the difference is between an UNPROFOR convoy and a humanitarian aid convoy? Can you explain that to that Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that while all convoys were generally escorted by UNPROFOR, and as evidenced by the documents that I think I discussed during the Prosecution case, you could see two separate classes of convoys that would be moving via the roads. One set of convoys was specifically limited to the supply and provisioning of the designated United Nations military forces in the enclaves or in other areas of Bosnia. And the other set of convoys were those by other United Nations aid agencies or other humanitarian organisations that would be going into the enclaves for their own purposes. So those are the two general categories of convoys that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know from which type of convoys was it possible to extract certain quantities of fuel oil to be used by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would presume that both. For example, in one of the documents that was discussed related to an UNPROFOR convoy, the Bosnian Serb military showed concern about wanting to verify the exact amount of fuel in each military vehicle because of their concern that they would be travelling into the enclaves with far more fuel than they actually needed to complete one rotation in and out of the enclave. And the concern was, you know, ABiH military forces would then just siphon off the extra fuel. It would just come right out of the military fuel tanks. In the case of the other UN convoys, one, the same method would apply as well as other more overt situations where fuel and other things would be improperly manifested so that it would show a lesser amount on the manifest document that was actually carried. Those were both concerns that the Bosnian military had with respect to a means of getting fuel into the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you referring to ABiH army when you said the Bosnian army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess I am referring to both. As you're aware, certainly within the context of the VRS at Srebrenica, the Bosnian Muslim military was perceived as getting fuel from UN sources and by their own documents in the Zepa enclave, the Bosnian Serb military was obtaining fuel from the Ukrainian Detachment there that was also operating under United Nations auspices. So I guess within the context of fuel, both parties were surreptitiously obtaining fuel from United Nations sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I did understand the difference between the two types of convoys, but I would like to know all those convoys from humanitarian convoys had they to be escorted by UNPROFOR elements or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the convoys originate from Sarajevo, and those areas did pick up a UN escort. I am not sure whether or not humanitarian convoys, and many did originate from Belgrade to the eastern enclaves, whether they actually had a United Nations escort or whether they were allowed to travel independently. So I don't know the answer to the second part of the question with respect to convoys coming out of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, you have moved on to black marketeering.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D607 and see what the UNPROFOR deputy commander in Srebrenica has to say about it, Mr. Robert Franken, who was also chief of logistics. It's P607. P607. Thank you. That's Mr. Franken's statement. We need page 2 in Serbian, paragraph -- paragraphs 3 and 4; and page 1, paragraphs 3 and 4 in English. He says: "In that period of time, the Serbs suggested to the Muslims that they should trade with the Muslims based on the prices that existed on the black market in the enclave. When I say 'trade,' I mean trade with all -- all [indiscernible] except for the weapons. After several rounds of negotiations, the civilian authorities of the enclave gave their approval for the goods to be supplied by the Serbs to the enclave. We insisted that the goods be sold in the enclave for roughly the market price and that DutchBat should claim no commercial role in this." This next paragraph: "This fitted well with our idea of bringing the relations between the warring parties back to normal. Rumors spread that the initiative was not viewed well by the groups that controlled the black market. The trade was put a stop to by the military leadership. It was said by the local military leadership that the prohibition had come from the top of the military leadership, although such things worked well in Gorazde, and I presume that the initiative to boycott the trade had really come from the military leadership of the enclave."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Did you come across any documents relating to the two parties trading, and can you tell us why did the Srebrenica military leadership accommodate the requests coming from individuals involved in the black market?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did come across documents as well as statements from various individuals which did discuss the proposals to kind of normalise trade in and out of the enclaves. My understanding is not only for their purposes the Bosnian Muslim side did not agree to that, and I suspect that black marketeering would be a motive. There are a number of reports that members of the 28th Infantry Division in general, and Naser Oric in particular, were making a very good living with respect to black market operations in the enclave. From the Bosnian Serb side, the idea of normalising trade with the civilians with -- inside the enclave kind of ran counter to their idea of creating the conditions necessary to force the people out of the enclave. So while I take it that the local civilians on both sides of the enclave would be in support of this proposal, I understand that the military leadership on both sides was not eager to engage in a more normalising of commercial and trade relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I do understand that you were looking at the two sides in parallel, but you see that the document states that this system was in place in Gorazde and that they applied market prices. Was it the case that the market prices would not be agreeable to the black market operators, or, in fact, to the leadership of the VRS and the ABiH? We looked at the document which arrived from the Ministry of Defence of Srebrenica. What Franken says here, he is speaking as UNPROFOR deputy commander and chief of logistics, and he's referring to market prices. Should a parallel be drawn in every answer or should the document be rightly consulted for a proper answer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I mean in this particular case - and to be clear - from the ABiH side, their military leadership was accused of being the people who controlled the black market economy within the enclave. Their reasons were not broader than economic as to why they did not see a normalisation of trade activities. The military leadership of the VRS didn't view this in the context of black market or making themselves richer in the way that the ABiH military leadership in the enclave did. They were looking at it as more of a policy issue of not necessarily trading with the members of the enclave because in making their lives potentially easier, they were running counter to their own policy of wanting to create the conditions to leave. Both sides shared the motive of not wanting to see trade normalised but for entirely different reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you, yourself, come across a document originating from the Serb side which discusses this issue? Can you refer to a document that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a number of years, but I seem to recall there was at least one document. I don't know whether it was authored by Momir Nikolic or he was just part of the conversation where the issue was discussed -- or he was aware the issue was discussed relating to normalising trade and that the local community in Bratunac -- the civilian leadership in Bratunac was not necessarily opposed to that because they believed that by trading with the civilians in the enclave, they could actually get supplies and goods from them that they could not obtain from Serbia due to the embargo, particularly fuel. And as part of those discussions, the military leadership indicated that they were not prepared to permit that. So I'm aware of at least one document, like I said, it's been few years, where those issues are discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. My request of you was to refer us to any document which indicates that the Serb position was, as indicated by Mr. Franken here -- and if you could do so at any point during your testimony. Now, let's go back to the issue at hand which is the control of convoys by UNPROFOR, and I'm referring to humanitarian aid convoys. Can you tell us -- or, rather, let me put it differently: Who was it who had the right to control UNPROFOR humanitarian aid convoys and humanitarian aid convoys organised by various international organisations? I mean, who within the UN had the right to control these convoys to make sure that they did not include weapons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, referring to my previous answer on that, I am not aware under every circumstance who was responsible for ensuring that every single convoy was properly manifested and that weapons were not being put in. I assume that for those UNPROFOR convoys that were going to resupply their own units that those responsibilities would be taken by the UNPROFOR forces that were organising the convoys. With respect to the other humanitarian aid convoys, I don't know whether or not those organisations were themselves responsible for insuring that weapons did not get into those convoys, or whether or not they had to submit their vehicles and manifests for inspection by UNPROFOR before those requests were consolidated and sent to the Republika Srpska for approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at document P10111 [as interpreted] in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before it appears, can you tell us this: Did UNPROFOR control UNHCR convoys as they emerged in the enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, again, the actual specifics of whether or not they were controlled by UNPROFOR, whether they were merely escorted by the UNPROFOR, or how much or how little control that the UN protection forces exerted over the actual UN convoys. I just don't know the detail of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On our screens we have the Agreement on Complete Cessation of Hostilities. Under 3 the agreement reads -- I'm sorry, Article 5: "Full freedom of movement with appropriate procedures shall exist for UNPROFOR and other official international agencies, in particular UNHCR, in order to complement this agreement, to monitor human rights and to deliver humanitarian aid, including medical supplies and evacuations. The parties commit themselves to full respect for the safety and security of UNPROFOR and related personnel. UNPROFOR shall continue to prevent any abuse of freedom of movement by its personnel or convoys which might be of military benefit to either party." The article I've read out deals with a number of issues, but we were only interested in the abuse of convoys. So my question is: Who has it within their authority to monitor the abuse of convoys of humanitarian aid organised by either UNPROFOR or other international organisations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, this document is P1011 and not P10111. Now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And again maybe it's a matter of translation, but when I read the last sentence it says: "The UNPROFOR shall continue to prevent any abuse of freedom of movement by its personnels or convoys which might be of military benefit to either party." I take that that the UNPROFOR is responsible for the conduct of its convoys and personnel. I don't know if I'd link that to the first sentence which is that the UNPROFOR would also ensure that UNHCR personnel and convoys also did not conduct the same. It may be the case. I just -- I don't know and I don't think it's clear from this particular passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that UNPROFOR was able not to prevent the abuse of UNHCR convoys or its own convoys if they happen to find that mines and explosives are being smuggled in them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I don't know enough of how that process worked to be able to give you or the Court an answer as to whether or not there was a regime available that the UNPROFOR actually inspected other agency convoys to ensure that that was not happening, or whether those other international agencies were expected to police themselves. I have to assume that if the UNPROFOR became aware of a UNHCR or other international convoy that was carrying prescribed military equipment instead of carrying humanitarian or civilian goods that they would not have let that travel, but I don't know that they viewed that as their job that they were going to inspect each and every convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But was it possible for UNPROFOR to find anything out if they did not conduct checks? And what sort of method was employed by UNPROFOR in respect of the convoys they escorted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, from the UNPROFOR side, their particular convoys, as evidenced by the manifests that we have, they were required in a great amount of detail to lay out the entire cargos and personnel manifests of each convoy going into the enclaves, submit them to the Republika Srpska and the Main Staff for approval, and they understood that at some point those convoys were also going to be subject to inspection, and that if there was excess equipment or fuel or equipment that was not properly manifested that the convoy could be turned around or those possessions confiscated. I don't know how that process worked with the other aid agencies, whether or not they had as sophisticated an apparatus to verify what was going into those vehicles or not, and I don't know what the inspection regime would have been until it got into the Republika Srpska. Now, obviously, just with the UNPROFOR convoys, the humanitarian convoys from other agencies had to manifest their equipment and were also subject to inspection by the VRS at various check-points. And as we know from various documents, in cases where equipment was identified that was not properly manifested or wasn't manifested at all, the VRS confiscated that equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, please, as a military analyst, the inspection of humanitarian convoys and UNPROFOR convoys at check-points, was it not one of the methods of preventing abuse? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. The Bosnian Serb military saw the ability to inspect these various convoys at various places as an important means by which they could assure themselves that prescribed military equipment or other dual-use type of supplies or supplies that were not -- or that were being sent in excess of what the perceived civilian needs were could be controlled. So they were very much involved in that process because they saw it as an important way to control the amount of supplies that went into the eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago, we quoted Article 5 of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. As a military analyst, do you find it acceptable that this should be the basis for an agreement between UNPROFOR and the VRS? Because it does provide in great detail the freedom of movement to be accorded to UNPROFOR convoys. In other words, is it the basis for the freedom of movement of convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular agreement does lay out the principles relating to freedom of movement. And, again, with the fact that the expectation is that, you know, all parties would allow for the freedom of movement on the one hand, and on the other hand that with respect to the UNPROFOR and the other aid agencies, that they would not allow their offices to be used for military purposes by either one of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up document D77 in e-court. It's an agreement which was signed on behalf of UNPROFOR by General Brinkman and on behalf of the VRS, General Zdravko Tolimir. We see here item 1 which reads: "These principles define the appropriate procedures regarding freedom of movement, as stated in paragraph 5 of the Agreement on Complete Cessation of Hostilities, signed on the 31st of December, 1994. These principles specifically refer to UNPROFOR movements on Serb held territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Is this first item completely based on Article 5 of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, is that the case? And you did look at the other agreement.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean, and I believe that's explicitly laid out in paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to paragraph 2 which relates to the obligation of mutual reporting, that is to say, the obligation of UNPROFOR to notify issues to the Main Staff. So we're dealing with notification in A; we're dealing with movement in B; and in C, with the approval for movement which is to be given by the Main Staff. Did the Main Staff, in fact, grant approval to UNPROFOR vehicles to transit the territory under their control?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As we've noted from the documents during the Prosecution case, there were various lists of convoy movements projected, many were approved, some were disapproved, many others had their cargos modified but they were given subsequent approval. So within that context, the process did work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see that under 3 the agreement envisages control, and it reads: "Convoys may be checked only once by a Serbian Army check-point," or "for an army. This regards both the incoming and outgoing convoy movement. The inspection of the convoy will last as short as possible. If goods not stated on the notification are found, a more detailed check will be made. "Goods not mentioned on the notification will be allowed to return on their convoy to their starting points. Goods which are not notified and for which transport is forbidden will be taken into secure storage." And the reference here is to mines and explosives: "A joint control by the warring parties," that's to say the two armies and UNPROFOR, on the other hand, "will discuss the final decision regarding these goods. A list of forbidden goods will be handed over to UNPROFOR by the Serbian army HQ, Main Staff." Tell us, was the Army of Republika Srpska entitled to fully inspect convoys both the humanitarian convoys and United Nations convoys? Is this not regulated herein?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, from the part of this document I can see, what they are discussing here is the UNPROFOR convoys. I don't know how limited this particular document is. I mean, one of the things that strikes me is that it talks about there being a separate agreement, even within the United Nations framework, between this document which is covering the UNPROFOR and a subset of the UN forces which is the United Nations military observers. So again, I take that this document deals specifically with the UNPROFOR. I don't know if its provisions broadly extend to all UN agencies. As to your second question, yes, as discussed, it sets up a framework by which the Army of Republika Srpska will have an opportunity to inspect convoys going in and out in order to ensure that there is no abuse of the process and that the convoys are carrying only their manifested cargo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's time for the break. Mr. Tolimir, before we break, I would just like to note that you have read, especially paragraph 3, into the record, but not literally, especially in relation to this abbreviation "SA." We see in the first line "SA check-point," and later on, second part of paragraph 3, "A joint SA UNPROFOR commission." Your interpretation of that was of the word "warring party." That might be right, that can be wrong. At the end in the last line we see: "UNPROFOR by the Serbian army HQ." SA could be an abbreviation for Serbian army which is, in the context of our discussion, quite strange. I just put it on the record to make sure that we all check the real meaning of SA. We have to adjourn now and we will resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Or, I see Mr. McCloskey on his feet. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I was just informed -- well, in the last session via e-mail that literally as I was standing withdrawing those four witnesses, one of the witnesses finally contacted our person and said that they would be available any time. And that is Witness number 95, PW-29, and we have been able to schedule that witness September 12th. It's a 92 ter witness. It should be very short, but an important witness. So if I could move the Court to withdraw my previous withdrawal and place that witness back on the witness list, and we'll put him in the schedule as we're confirming with him right now, I would appreciate that. I apologise. It's just one of those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is there any concern by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no objection to this witness appearing in the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, your withdrawal of the withdrawal is accepted. You may call the witness. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, since before the break we were looking at the Agreement on the Cessation of Hostilities and we quoted Article 5 therein, do I need to show the document again to you or can you answer my question now? Was the Agreement on Complete Cessation of Hostilities stipulate the forming of a central joint submission in order to oversee the implementation of the agreement and was that carried out in practice?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, as the document has come up, paragraph 2 of that agreement calls for the creation of a central joint commission. Taking that on to the following document, that appears to be at least with respect to -- at least -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need the previous page in B/C/S, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Tolimir is not receiving the translation into B/C/S; therefore, he did not hear the answer provided by Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, could you be so kind to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The document that is currently up on the screen, paragraph 2, calls for the establishment of joint commissions. I believe the following document is the attempt to implement that with at least respect to the Bosnian Serb military and the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now see this document, D250, which speaks about the forming of a joint central commission as well as regional commissions. Thank you. Let's see how and at whose initiative the agreement was drafted, the agreement that was signed. Here we see a document produced by the Main Staff dated the 5th of January, 1995. It is addressed from the meeting of the central state commission to the addressees as listed herein, and on the last page we can see that the document was signed by General Tolimir. Now, please, I am interested in item 5 of this agreement which reads that: "UNPROFOR will prepare a draft of an agreement to be agreed by the signed."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the item read by Mr. Tolimir does not correspond to item 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Tolimir please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please repeat your question. The interpreters didn't interpret it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in this item 5 that I have just quoted, does it specify the manner in which the agreement had been concluded on freedom of movement, concluded on the 31st of January, 1995, between General Brinkman, the representative of UNPROFOR, and General Tolimir, the representative of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm looking at the same paragraph 5, it -- all it specifically says is that the UNPROFOR will prepare a draft agreement on complete freedom of movement which will be agreed bilaterally with the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's correct. And I would like to hear your opinion because this is a report from a meeting by a joint commission which says, under 5, that it was agreed for UNPROFOR to prepare a draft agreement on freedom of movement to be agreed bilaterally. Was this agreement agreed bilaterally between Brinkman and Tolimir? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure that I accept your proposition that this is merely a report of a meeting. There are other portions of the document which you appear to have added a considerable amount of commentary with respect to what you believe that various negotiating positions would be, as well as what the position of the VRS should be or would be in response. I take it that at some juncture the agreement was signed, but I don't -- like I said, I mean, just looking at spots of this document rather than having the entire document, it's very difficult for me to conclude exactly what it is in its entirety and what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I was not asking you about the contents of the whole document. I was specifically asking you about item 5, whether it specifically determines the manner in which this agreement on complete freedom of movement of UNPROFOR was to be achieved. Does it say who is to prepare the draft of this document? And I am talking about item 5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The nature of that question requires Mr. Butler to be able to understand the document, and it does no good for the witness to just repeat what is said in the paragraph. So if the General wants a serious evaluation I would allow him to let Mr. Butler review the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would suggest that we go back to the other document, to the agreement itself, to see if this item 5 of this document is from the content reflected in the agreement itself. Can we go back to -- I suggest that you call for that document again, D77.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I said D77. To which part of this agreement do you refer, Mr. Tolimir? That would be helpful for the witness to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I made reference to the manner in which an agreement was reached between UNPROFOR and the VRS concerning the territory of the VRS, and for that purpose I proposed the previous document in order to see what was the role of UNPROFOR. On several occasions there was discussion before about the fact that the VRS was said to have imposed this and that checks -- what I wanted to prove was that it was something that was requested or required by the UNPROFOR. I could show the witness the whole document, however, I cannot quote it in its entirety. I can only quote specific items. For example, item 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. This was not my intention. You put a question to the witness: "Does it say who it was to prepare the draft of this document?" That was your question put to the witness. It would be helpful for the witness to know to which part of the agreement you are referring, to understand item 5 of your letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am talking about the whole agreement proposed to the VRS to be signed regarding the freedom of movement of UNPROFOR throughout the whole territory of Republika Srpska, and I am talking about the manner in which it was constructed, and I demonstrated that by quoting item 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you able to answer this specific question in relation to item 5 of the document signed by Mr. Tolimir, D250, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe, if I am correct, what General Tolimir is referring to is that in paragraph 5 of that document it states that the UNPROFOR will draft the principles for the agreement of movement, and then what we are now looking at on the screen is, in fact, the manifestation of that draft. I take it -- I hope that's what General Tolimir was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we go back to D254. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is the wrong number. We saw D250; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that we should go back to D254 before we go to the one that we have on the screens. All right. Now we have it and we have item 5. Now let us look at the first page of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just to clarify so that we have a clear record. This is D250 which we have on the screen with item 5. If you want to have on the screen another document, you should not say "let's go back" to that document, because we didn't have it on the screen yet. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Mr. President. We hadn't had D254 before. It was just a minor administrative error, so we are seeking to look at 254.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, here we see a document made by the Main Staff of the VRS, the sector for intelligence and security affairs. It was produced on the 12th of February, 1995. It was sent to all the commands, and it speaks about the movement of UNPROFOR around the territory of Republika Srpska. In paragraph 1, it says: "Through the regional joint commissions UNPROFOR representatives are constantly bringing up the issue of greater freedom of movement for UNPROFOR across the front line, with the aim of getting authorisation to cross the front line and move within the territory of Republika Srpska on the lower regional levels while not having to notify the Main Staff and not to having to wait for authorisation by the Main Staff of the VRS before doing so. "This kind of approach indicates that UNPROFOR wanted to avoid the obligation undertaken by them in the agreement signed on the principles of freedom of movement signed on the 31st of January, 1995, between the UNPROFOR command and General Tolimir, and the text of that agreement is attach hereto." Now, what comes next is the agreement that we already looked at. Now, let's move to this portion where you say that I was making some comments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we need page 2 where we see -- we need page 2. Thank you. Can I have page 2 in e-court, please. In English, it's page 3. And can we scroll down the text in the Serbian because I would like to read the last sentence on page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR representatives during -- concluding the agreement, insisted that their goods not be seized, that is possibly not listed in the notification due to an administrative error, and they conceded that under such circumstances they would return the whole convoy to its points of departure. We agreed as -- with that as can be seen from the agreement, but we emphasised that the items that were not listed in the manifest and whose transportation is forbidden would be confiscated and kept in our depots until a conclusion reached about what to do with them by the joint commission." My question is: These joint military commissions, were they authorised to inspect the routes and the checks and the arrival of UNPROFOR convoys that had previously been notified to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand this particular document correctly with the last one, it was not the joint military commissions themselves which conducted the inspections, it was the joint military commission that created the framework agreement. The actual inspection of the materials would be left to each individual party. So, you know, in that context it was not like there was a joint United Nations Republika Srpska military check-point which cleared each convoy -- or physically inspected each convoy. The military commission created the framework as to how it would be done, but, you know, the UN was left to manifest the convoy, the VRS Main Staff approve the convoy, and it would be inspected by a VRS check-point at an agreed upon location.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, after reading this item in the last question which says that the final decision -- pending final decision, the goods would be kept in our depots; that is to say, the pending decision to be taken by the joint commission. So does that mean that these joint commissions had to be notified about any cargos that had been seized and stored in depots? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way that this particular document lays that out goes into, first, laying out that there will be lists that will be made as to what cargos -- or the transport of cargos that are prohibited. The third paragraph from the end notes a request from General Tolimir to subordinated formations requesting that they forward a draft list of the cargos that they think need to be banned, and that once this is done they will actually public the full list. The last part of the process will be: Should cargos be pulled off of convoys? This document does call for them to be put into a depot and maintained in that depot until such a point in time as a joint decision has been made as to what the status of the cargo is. So this document kind of lays out an ongoing process in light of the fact that it lays out a broader process on here's how this cargo will be handled, but acknowledges in the very next paragraph that at the point in time that this document is written there is not a list yet of what that prescribed cargo is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Can you please answer me this: Who is to take the decision relating to the items confiscated at check-points and toward in depots? Was that decision to be taken by the joint military commission or somebody else? And I'm referring to the decision that you talked about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe from the contents of the document that the decision to actually remove cargo from a convoy and place it in a depot would be made by the party that was inspecting the convoy. The ultimate disposition of that cargo once it got to the depot as to whether or not it would be brought back to United Nations custody or whether it would be allowed to continue on to the enclave or its destination, or a third option that it remains in the depot, would presumably be made by that joint military commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were then members of the joint military commission who were supposed to decide on this required to be informed about all the items that were banned, seized, confiscated, stored, et cetera? Did the members of the joint military commission have to know about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect that at some point after the publication of this document that once a list was established by the VRS and once cargo was being -- one, that list would have obviously been passed to the joint military commissions so all parties would know what cargo could not travel through. And then to the next step in instances where such cargo was confiscated, in order to come to a conclusion as to what to do with that cargo, one would think that members of the joint commission would have to be informed of its seizure, the circumstances of its seizure, and the fact that the cargo was, in fact, part of the list of banned cargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If General Tolimir was a member of this joint commission and a signatory to this agreement, was it necessary for him to be informed about the documents that indicated that parts of convoys were banned, seized, or in any other way hampered with? Was it necessary for him to be informed fully about that and sign any kind of documents in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: While you could have taken a personal interest in this, it would also have been appropriate for you to delegate the responsibility for implementing this to another member of the Main Staff. It could have been within the security branch or intelligence branch or it could have even been with the approval of General Milovanovic or General Mladic, another member of the Main Staff who might have been more suited to the role. So I don't believe that you would have had to personally do this, but it could have been delegated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I think this was not the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "If Mr. Tolimir was a member of this joint commission, should he be notified about this specific cargo which was seized?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he were the functioning member, he would have to be notified, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, that was the question. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Does this agreement signed by Tolimir and Brinkman on freedom of movement of UNPROFOR regulate the movement of convoys belonging to other humanitarian organisations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure. I believe that if you go back to the agreement it did specifically make a differential between the UNPROFOR and the UNMO convoys. So, again, I am not sure from the parts of the agreement that we've reviewed whether or not that agreement covered the entirety of other humanitarian organisation convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us please look at the last paragraph of the document, just above the signature block. It reads: "These freedom of movement principles refer only to convoys and single UNPROFOR vehicles and not to convoys of international humanitarian organisations. Regarding convoys of international humanitarian organisations, they should implement the procedure and checks agreed upon so far." So, therefore, my question: The agreement signed by Tolimir and Brinkman, did it refer only to individual UNPROFOR convoys? I mean, convoys and individual UNPROFOR vehicles. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I take it from this last paragraph that the interpretation of the VRS and of General Tolimir was that this particular agreement was limited only to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As a military analyst who has been able to read the agreement in the course of your testimony today, so is it only my interpretation that this agreement relates to UNPROFOR alone? You are of a different opinion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe that you're speaking on behalf of the VRS when you're making this interpretation of what this agreement covers. I don't believe it's just singularly your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did UNPROFOR interpret the agreement as written in the various items that it contains?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to the context by which UNPROFOR believed the agreement, whereas what it covered or what it did not. I mean, all I can tell you, again, going back to the agreement, was that as a context of the agreement the UNPROFOR covered their convoy movements and it specified out that the UNMOs would be separate. If there is a separate -- or if there is a third or fourth page in the basic agreement that notes that you -- the international convoys were covered, that's one thing. If it's not, I would assume that they are not covered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Let's go back to D77 in order for you to see what we are discussing. Thank you. Have a look at the document which relates to the freedom of movement principles. It was issued by the Main Staff of the BH command in Sarajevo. You can see that there is their letterhead. It speaks of the aims -- the aim, under 1; notification, 2; control, under 3, and the way it is to be exerted; under 4, the notification of roots.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the next page please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would ask in this situation that these documents be printed out, these multipage documents be printed out, and Mr. Butler have a chance to review them. I can't follow what is going on here. This electronic way of going from one page to the next, to the next and back, Mr. Butler is trying but -- and then being quizzed on the last paragraph of one document. If he wants a serious evaluation or analysis of this document, I would ask that it be printed out, to have him allowed to have two different documents printed out for him so he can do some sort of reasonable analysis. This is completely confusing. I don't know what he is being asked about, where he is going from, which document. This computer, unfortunately, doesn't make this very easy. And I know Mr. Butler is trying, but he cannot be expected to be able to answer questions clearly in this kind of a format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Registrar already printed it out, the agreement. It should be handed over to the witness if everybody agrees with this procedure. I don't see any objection. Yes, please hand it over to Mr. Butler. This is the agreement itself, D77. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We'll give Mr. Butler a chance to review the agreement, and we'll ask him to tell us if it relates to UNPROFOR convoys and vehicles alone or to others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's a simple question: Who does the agreement apply to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the absence of any language in this particular agreement relating to other humanitarian convoys, I take it that the agreement specifically deals with the issue of the UNPROFOR convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show 65 ter 5717. Thank you. It has appeared. It's a VRS Main Staff document, dated the 21st of August -- or, rather, 31st of August. Apologies. Thank you, Aleksandar. The 31st of August. It is signed by deputy commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milovanovic, and it is titled: "Order Regarding Movement of Humanitarian Aid Across Separation Lines."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will quote from paragraph 1 and then we can discuss it. It reads: "You know that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska no longer has any jurisdiction or responsibility concerning approval of entry and movement of teams and convoys of organisations through the territory of Republika Srpska. "This approval is issued by the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid and the Ministry of Health, Labour, and Social Welfare." This is my question: While reviewing the documents as part of your preparations, did you contemplate what the competence was of the Main Staff and what the competence was of other bodies, such as the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a three-page document in English. We heard that it was from some lieutenant-colonel. Could Mr. Butler be at least allowed to see the whole page -- the whole document if he is going to be asked about it and see who it is from?
