Because it is hard for me to imagine that this is from a lieutenant-colonel, but perhaps it is. I can't see the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed it would be --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. This is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- helpful for the witness to see the whole document. If you put such a broad question about the whole content of this document to the witness, then the witness should have the possibility to look at it. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And of course, we do see it is from Lieutenant-General Milovanovic. So just if we could have the whole document so he can do it, because otherwise between the translations and the piecemeal approach it's going to be very difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. President. As I was announcing the document, I said that it was sent by a deputy commander, Lieutenant-General Manojlo Milovanovic. Perhaps the witness did hear it or perhaps it wasn't interpreted. And then I quoted from paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Because of the discussions we've had, I would like to repeat my question. Did the VRS Main Staff give approval for the movement of humanitarian convoys or was it only competent to issue such approvals for UNPROFOR convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this kind of illustrates exactly why I would like to look at the whole document. If you look at that paragraph or that page in isolation, you can make that assertion. If you look at the last page where we looked at the signature, there looked like an order from General Milovanovic that part of it looked like they were specifically issuing orders that were not in compliance with that, and there is a middle page that I haven't even seen. So context matters, and to be able to make an assessment as to, you know, based on one line of a three-page document that this is the way it was, when I'm looking at the third page of the document and it appears they are trying to subvert that, it kind of seems like to be a bit of a pointless exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should take that comment of Mr. Butler into account and try to rephrase your questions or give the witness the opportunity to look through the entire document, otherwise it's not helpful for your Defence. Please carry on. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on your examination and take into consideration the best way to get a good answer from this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, what was the authority of this co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid at the time this document was written on the 1st [as interpreted] of August, 1994?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure of the specific responsibilities for the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid. It was not an issue that I looked very deeply into.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 21st [as interpreted] of August, 1994, as General Milovanovic states in the introductory part of its order, the approval would be given by the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid in the Ministry of Health, Labour, and Social Welfare. Was this body indeed authorised to give approvals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were interpreted to having said "21st of August, 1994." The document is from the 31st of August, 1994. I don't see a reference to another date in the document as we see it on the screen. Could you [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I sometimes do not articulate clearly what I say, so the interpreters may have misheard what I said. The date is the 31st of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, do you recall the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I can answer it. As noted in the paragraph on the first page, it specifically notes that the approval is now issued by the co-ordinating body. So I take it from General Milovanovic's authorship of this document that they are the accepted authority to issue approvals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As we can see in item 3 where the obligations of the Army of Republika Srpska are listed, can you tell us did the VRS have the right to control and inspect such convoys moving along the territory under the control of the VRS? It's paragraph 3, I misspoke when I said item 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are referring to paragraph 3 of the first page; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you're correct that paragraph 3 specifically states that the Army of Republika Srpska has the obligation to check teams and convoys of humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You are now able to see the preamble to the order.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 so that Mr. Butler may have a chance to look through the entire document as requested by the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, having examined the document, can you tell us does it clearly transpire from the document that all the information concerning the humanitarian convoys, the VRS should be conveyed to the VRS through the notification sent to them from the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid and the Ministry of Health, Labour, and Social Welfare?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the document specifically notes in paragraph 1 of the order is that regardless of the circumstances, that military forces are not to permit convoys to go into territory under the control of Muslim or Croatian forces if the crossing has not been announced in writing by the Main Staff of the VRS. So I take that to mean that even if the humanitarian co-ordinating body -- if such a convoy has the authority of the co-ordinating humanitarian body, unless there is also confirmation of that issued by the army that the army is not to allow these convoys to pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put a question to the witness at this point in time to understand the discussion more clearly. I take it that this is an order of the deputy commander of the Main Staff of the VRS to subordinate units. Mr. Butler, can you help us, is this exactly in accordance with an agreement between the VRS and UNPROFOR? Have you any idea about that, the connection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- between this ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe they are connected. This particular document, I belive, refers strictly to other humanitarian convoys that were run by either other UN agencies or other international agencies. I don't believe that this particular document -- and it's tough to tell because this is August 1994 and the agreement we are talking about is dated January 1995. But I believe that these protocols are dealing strictly with humanitarian goods that would be more under the purview of control of civilian organs of the RS as opposed to the UNPROFOR which would be more under the purview of control of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct that this document is an internal order from the Main Staff of the VRS to subordinate units in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go back to page 1 of the document in e-court to paragraph 4. I would like to quote it for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have a look at this. I did ask you if the notifications were the source of information for the Army of Republika Srpska and for the check-points conducting these checks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand what you are asking with respect to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the VRS receive information about humanitarian convoys from the co-ordinating body in order to be able to check the cargo the convoys carried and if it was indeed the cargo that had been approved?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the context of this document, page 1, I mean, it notes that they are receiving information, as you said in paragraph 4. And it also notes that in the following paragraph that they acknowledge that the information that they are receiving is often incomplete and they are doing the best that they can in order to receive the additional information that they believe that they and the corps need in order to allow these things to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order for us to move to another document, I would like first to tender this document into evidence and then I would seek another document to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 5717 shall be assigned Exhibit D303. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have in e-court P689. As we can see this is an Official Gazette. We need page 2 in the Serbian and keep page 1 in English, please. This is about in -- as it says in Article 1, that a decision was taken to set up a state committee for co-operation with United Nations and international humanitarian organisations. And then in Article 3, it is said: "Decisions and orders from the committee's jurisdiction are obligatory for all state organs of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on this, my question is as follows: Did you know that there was a commission existing in Republika Srpska, a state committee for co-operation with the United Nations and international humanitarian organisations and that its decisions were binding for everyone, including the Army of Republika Srpska? Did you see anything to that effect in the documents that you reviewed and studied?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask you to go to page 2 in the English language of this please, for a second? The next page. The next page down, please, also. Third. Okay. I guess where I am confused is -- and that's why I wanted to check the actual date of the decree, was that we are discussing from the prior document something in 31 August of 1994, and we're referring now to a decree published on 15 March 1995, and I am not sure if they are even related or not. I mean, I understand generally your question, Was there an organ to do that? Yes, there was. But I am not sure that this particular document which is published five -- six months after the August document that you referred to relates to it, or relates to maybe a prior iteration of that organ. So I am not sure where you are getting at with the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May we please see the top of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe if we read Article 6 that would be helpful for Mr. Butler because he wants to understand the whole document. Let's see what Article 6 of this decision says, and I quote: "Permits for the movement of convoys and employees of the United Nations and humanitarian organisations on the territory of Republika Srpska shall be issued by the co-ordinating body for humanitarian operations, pursuant to this committee's decisions." Now we can take a look at the decision taken by the committee with respect to the co-ordinating body, and I would like to hear whether there was a link between the co-ordinating body and this committee.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure. I go to Article 11 where it specifically notes that: "On the day of the publication on this decision, the decision on forming a state committee for co-operation with the UNPROFOR and all previously adopted enactments relating to the work of the committee shall become null and void if they are contrary to this decision." So I gather the answer to the question is if the Republika Srpska authorities did not consider the work of that commission or committee to be contrary to this decree, they would be related, and if they did consider the work to be contrary, they would not be related. And I don't know the answer to that question one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: Did all the state organs have an obligation to co-ordinate their work with regard to international humanitarian organisations in compliance with this decision? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I have the ability to answer that question. I did not study the workings of the state organs with respect to this particular regulation or document and how they worked with the UN. That's outside my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you dealt with the issue of convoys, and you said that in examination-in-chief, did you study all the laws and bylaws that pertain to this area and governed the movement of international organisations and their convoy across the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What I had studied was the practical application of the process whereby which the United Nations protection forces would submit convoy clearances to the Main Staff and the decision-making process of the Main Staff in granting the clearance for the convoy to move or making changes in the manifest or denying permission for the convoy to travel. That was the focus of my review of that material. It was not to encompass all of the other legal and diplomatic ramifications beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you answered several questions in examination-in-chief about humanitarian convoys and the approvals and denials of their passage, my question is: The decisions and orders issued by this commission or committee, did they apply to everyone in Republika Srpska that had anything to do with humanitarian convoys and humanitarian organisations? Thank you. As a jurist, I would like you to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness answered this question already. He said he didn't study all the internal regulation and beyond this area of his investigation. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you think that in order to analyse humanitarian convoys, it is essential to be familiar with the legal provisions pertaining to a specific territory that you are studying?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of what I was asked to do by the Office of the Prosecutor, the legal underpinnings and the diplomatic underpinnings of convoy movements, in my mind, were not necessary to know. What I was asked to do was to look at particular convoy documents with the first goal of making a determination as to whether or not the VRS Main Staff was actively involved in the process of reviewing them and clearing them, which my assessment is that they were; and secondly, were the convoys that were not being cleared or was the materials that were being not manifested or being reduced, did they coincide with the stated policy of the VRS and the Republika Srpska with respect to Directive 7 and 7(1). For me to do that, I don't believe it's necessary for me to understand the legal and political aspects of negotiations between the Republika Srpska and the United Nations as to what laws are in effect covering convoy clearance and how the Republika Srpska civilian organs somehow interface with the Republika Srpska military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I quoted Article 3 to you on the forming of this state committee and I am going to repeat it: "The decisions and orders from the purview of the committee are binding for all the state organs of Republika Srpska." So if this committee gave its approval for a convoy to cross the territory of Republika Srpska, was that binding for the Army of Republika Srpska as one of its organs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The article says what it says. The decision and order from the committee's jurisdiction are obligatory on all state organs. The armed forces of the Republika Srpska would qualify as a state organ in this context. So in theory, what should have happened is if the committee improved in its entirety a particular convoy movement or a particular manifest by virtue of this document, the Main Staff would not have had the authority to modify manifests or to deny convoys that were cleared by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I also quoted Article 6, which speaks about the issuance of approvals for the movement of humanitarian convoys and UN and international organisations personnel through Republika Srpska is within the remit of the co-ordinating body. My question is: When we talk about issuing permits for the movement of convoys through Republika Srpska, was it something that the Main Staff was to be consulted or was it exclusively within the purview of the co-ordinating body mentioned herein?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a practical matter, the Main Staff would have had to have been consulted in this process because, ultimately speaking, the Main Staff and the military controlled access to the enclaves. They were -- as noted before, the enclaves had a significant military character. So the Main Staff, as the military arm of the Republika Srpska, has to be involved in this process very closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is as follows: In that case, did the state committee notify the Main Staff about what they approved or not approved because they were controlling the territory where the convoys travelled and whether they were crossing the lines into another territory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As evidenced by that 31 August 1994 document, they had to have co-ordinated that with the Main Staff because that document already lays out circumstances where convoys which had been cleared by various co-ordinating bodies, but not cleared by the Main Staff, were showing up at various parts of the battle-field. So there had to have been a process established; whereas, after a decision made by a civilian body on a humanitarian convoy was made, that ultimately that was co-ordinated with the military organs of the state because only the military organs of the state could ultimately ensure that the convoy could be cleared to pass through the territory and into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, was the Army of Republika Srpska supposed to tell the committee whether it was safe or not safe for a certain convoy to go down the specified route for which the committee gave its approval?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it that would be one purpose. One of the things that the committee would have to tell the army -- or that the army would be expected to tell the committee as to what routes that the convoy could take and at what times they would be cleared to be on those routes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's time for our second break. We adjourn and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you tell me when you were reviewing the documents relating to the convoys, did you come across any document testifying to the fact that the Main Staff failed to act in accordance with the decisions of the state committee and that it acted contrary to its decisions when it came to humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that I did off the top of my head. The general process, as I understand it, was the committee would -- once they approved a convoy, would then pass the material on to the Main Staff where they would ultimately clear the convoy for travel. There may have been cases where that has occurred, but I don't recall any off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are we talking about a permission or about an approval, and was the Main Staff obliged to abide by the decision taken by the committee regarding the passage of a convoy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's on a more technical basis. For example, along the lines of a convoy that may have been approved for a certain date did not travel or was not permitted to travel because they were entering into the Republika Srpska at a different check-point than had been cleared previously by the Main Staff. I know there were a number of cases like that. I don't believe it was the Main Staff itself overruling permission for convoys that had already been previously approved by the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what the difference is between the permission for movement across Republika Srpska and the approval for movement across front lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you -- in your question you've kind of laid out the differential. One process involved the actual approval of a convoy and its manifest. The second process revolved around gaining the necessary permission to cross the front lines or to enter the Republika Srpska at certain territories, most of which was controlled by the army; therefore, the VRS's involvement in that process, even with civilian United Nations agency convoys, was vital because as evidenced by the 31 October 1994 document -- I'm sorry, August 1994 document, they had to be appropriately cleared because you couldn't have a situation where United Nations convoys found themselves in a battle-field environment and nobody was aware that they were coming or that they were in the place that they were supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Did you have an opportunity to look at documents in which the secure conditions are provided for a convoy and where solutions are provided for some extraordinary situations that involved a degree of danger, if such situations occurred?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware, generally, that particularly with respect to convoys around Sarajevo, that that was a factor. I did not examine that particular issue closely given the fact that my primary focus was on convoys going into the eastern enclaves. So I -- and particularly Srebrenica and Zepa. So I agree in context. There were cases where the VRS refused to allow various convoys to pass because of claims of combat activity that was ongoing. But that was often not the issue with Srebrenica and Zepa. Those routes to those enclaves did not have constant combat in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D186, please. It's a document of the Main Staff dated the 12th of March, 1995, and it speaks about the prevention of plunder and looting because such things were happening. I am not going to read the whole document, only the first sentence from the introductory part. And it says: "The National Assembly of Republika Srpska and the highest organs of authority in Republika Srpska have verified the mandate of UNPROFOR in Republika Srpska. Since UNPROFOR is on a peace mission to Republika Srpska, (despite the fact that we - the Army of Republika Srpska and its Main Staff - as well other institutions in Republika Srpska have many objections to the biassed behaviour of UNPROFOR members, and there are regular discussions of this at the meetings held with the representatives of UNPROFOR) ..." And so on and so forth. And then it goes on to say at the end -- so in this introductory part it says that: "Regardless of the problems that we are facing, UNPROFOR is afforded legitimacy when it comes to its passing through the territory of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was whether this indicates that legitimacy is being afforded to UNPROFOR in the territory of Republika Srpska by invoking the authorities that granted them approval for deployment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we at least see who has written this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let's go to the last page in both versions. Signed by Colonel-General Ratko Mladic. Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In this context, it reflects the fact that while the Main Staff has issues with the UNPROFOR, the political powers of the state have affirmed the UNPROFOR's mission to be there and that they are to be accorded the respects and authorities that they are supposed to have under their mandate. So he acknowledges, you know -- on behalf of the army, you know, he acknowledges the status of the UNPROFOR in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 1 of the document back on our screens so that I can put my question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does paragraph 2, if you've read it, make reference to robbery being committed against members of UNPROFOR in the territory of Republika Srpska? In fact, that's how the paragraph starts: "There have been cases of UNPROFOR members being robbed in the past ..."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and, in fact, if you read that with the first paragraph on the second page, it lays out the proposition that there are not only individual acts of criminality perpetrated against the UNPROFOR but also groups of individuals who are doing that, and that because of the perception that the UNPROFOR is not neutral, that authorities within the army are not taking -- either not taking those reports seriously or not moving forward seriously to suppress banditry against the UNPROFOR because I think the phrase was people who are robbing UNPROFOR are actually true patriots. So it does lay out in the second paragraph the problems that they are having with these criminal bands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does not the order issuing authority condemn the sort of conduct you've referred to in paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, in the context it lays it out. I don't know if he specifically in that paragraph, you know, General Mladic condemns his actions, but certainly that's the point that is made that, you know, the military will not tolerate this behaviour. It's made in both paragraph 2 and paragraph 3. I would guess the top paragraph of the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll read paragraph 3 as well: "This and similar acts of robbery have in an inexplicable and unacceptable way become expressions of 'heroism' and manifestation of 'real' patriotism." In other words, he is drawing the attention to these problems. And now I'm moving on to read the order itself. "I hereby order --" thank you. I am unable to read the entire -- part 1. Yes, thank you: "Engaging all available forces, corps commanders shall order that searches be conducted and other actions taken in uncovering procedures with the aim of locating the perpetrators of these serious crimes, documenting the crimes, launching criminal proceedings against the perpetrators and returning UNPROFOR property." Does not item 1 of the order express in clear terms that all the envisaged criminal actions be taken against the perpetrators of such acts? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That -- the first part or paragraph 1 of that order lays out the corps commanders are responsible for dealing with the investigation issues related to locating the perpetrators of these crimes, documenting them, initiating criminal proceedings, and when recovery, obviously, to return the UNPROFOR property.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since corps commanders are mentioned here as the relevant structures, is that the case because they are the ones in charge of the entire territory through which UNPROFOR -- or, rather, convoys are supposed to pass?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part that is correct. The corps are the military units that ultimately control the territory. They are the geographically based ground forces. I would also direct your attention to paragraph 3 of that order because it's implied as part of the paragraph 3 that the other reason why the corps are involved is because there is at least the inference by the Main Staff that it may well be subordinate military commanders at the corps who are encouraging such acts. And as their commanders, the corps commanders would be expected to take active measures against these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that the Main Staff was able to make -- or give responsibility upon each and every corps commander if an act of robbery was committed in his area of responsibility to confer upon the responsibility to locate the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly, I don't know that it's the Main Staff had to give responsibility. It is my understanding under law that -- Republika Srpska law that existed at the time that the corps commanders themselves already had the authority to do that. But to the next point, General Mladic, as the commander of the army and whom the corps commanders were directly subordinate to, was making it clear personally, and when you look at paragraph 5 that he expected that the corps commanders would actively work to undertake this, these measures, and ensure that acts of robbery were not committed against the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Was it based on this that the army had its responsibilities in respect of convoys across the territory that it controlled, across Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess the answer is in part. I mean, when we go back to the issue of Directive 7 and Directive 7(1) where the issue of restricting UN convoys is discussed, it makes it clear that that is a thought out process of state and military policy. That's one aspect. This is an aspect dealing with individual and collective acts of criminalities. When you lay these two issues together it makes it clear that, you know, while the Army of Republika Srpska was going to engage in some activities as part of its state policy and part of its military programme against the United Nations protection forces, it was not, on the other hand, prepared to accept individual acts of criminality by rogue soldiers or rogue commanders in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. We will have time to look at what it is that Directive 7 and 7(1) have to say. Yesterday we were able to see that even General Smith received the announcement that -- of the fact that sanctions were going to be imposed in relation to the eastern enclaves. We will have an opportunity to discussion this. Let me ask you in relation to this specific document: Was this the reason why the army was supposed to receive announcements of the time, date, and route of convoys in order to timely redress any possible shortcomings or failures to take proper action in respect of convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been a reason, but I do not believe it was the primary reason. This is, again, simply put, the army taking actions to ensure that the UNPROFOR was not subject to criminal acts, particularly by members of the VRS. Now, obviously would the fact that the corps are advised as to when these convoys are going through or not, would that help in their crime prevention efforts? Certainly. But having said that, the fact is that the corps already had this information from well before March of 1995, so the fact that they are notifying the corps as to these issues of when these convoys pass and where, while potentially helpful to the crime prevention activities -- was more important for protecting the convoys and assuring their clearances through combat areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. That's a different issue. My question had to do with something else, but let's not waste time on this. I'd like to move to a different document. I don't want to waste time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D924 shown in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I should tell you that it's an -- it's a coded telegram sent by Akashi to Annan on the 1st of March, 1995, and it's entitled: "Attitude of the Bosnia Government to UNPROFOR." Paragraph 1 on page 1 reads: "The BiH has been increasingly intransigent toward the peace process and to UNPROFOR. Despite their acceptance of the cessation of hostilities agreement on 31st December 1994, and of the accords of several joint commissions held at the various command levels, the BiH has obstructed attempts by the UNPROFOR to improve liaison, observe confrontation lines, and separate forces by refusing to attend regularly the joint commission process. They have applied significant additional restrictions on UNPROFOR movement ..." This is my question: Did you have occasion to see a single document which would speak to the restriction imposed by the BH Army on the movement of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have seen individual documents related to that, but given the context of my particular analysis, the issue of movement restrictions by the BiH Army on the UNPROFOR, in any aspect outside of how it impacted the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves would not have been an area that I focussed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you perhaps examine the issue from the perspective of the fact that the central state commission is referred to as a central body through which the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement is being implemented as indicated by Mr. Akashi? He refers to the agreement of the 31st of December, 1994, and states that there were additional restrictions imposed on UNPROFOR movement. He also states that they no longer co-operated or worked with the joint commission. Did you have an opportunity to come across something like this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, while I may have come across it, the focus of my analysis in this area would have been related to the more tactical issue of restrictions of movement placed on the UNPROFOR forces within the enclaves and their impact on the ability of the UN forces within the enclaves to monitor all the activity in those enclaves. Those issues outside the enclaves wouldn't be relevant to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday we spoke of the restrictions of movement of liaison officers who were instituted as part of those cessation of hostilities agreement, and I'm quoting what Mr. Akashi has to say: "Numerous restrictions were imposed on UNPROFOR. The trend is that such restrictions are imposed at a time when armed activities are planned or when increased pressure is intended to be put on UNPROFOR." The last sentence says that they forced liaison officers to withdraw from Tuzla to Gornji Vakuf. We can see that in paragraph 3. And it was also indicated that those who were in Gornji Vakuf had to be transferred to the territory of Republika Srpska. This is my question: Since all these activities aimed toward restricting the movement of UNPROFOR and the control to be exerted by UNPROFOR over the BH Army were well known to both Annan and Akashi, does this mean that they did receive information from UNPROFOR units on the ground and UNPROFOR commanders about the activities of the BH Army and the violations of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement that they committed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one presumes that the information in this particular document is based on reporting from the ground commanders at the lowest levels in the UNPROFOR, and I believe it is, the notification inherent in this document would confirm what you've said, which is that that information that is occurring -- or those facts that are occurring on the ground are receiving visibility at the highest levels of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at paragraph 4 on page 3. Thank you. It reads: "There have also been several indicators which suggest that the BiH is considering an offensive in the near future." Under A: "The refusal of the BiH to accept the BSA liaison officers is referred to." Under B, it reads there are indicators that the BiH is improving its efficiency through reorganisation, rearming training and force standardisation. Mobilisation of large numbers of troops continues in the major centres of Zenica and Tuzla. There has been unusually heavy troop movement and resupply towards the northern regions. Hospitals on the western confrontation line have been warned to expect casualties. This is my question: Did the United Nations precisely identify which was the side that refused to continue complying with the cessation of hostilities agreement and that continued with combat activities on the territory under its control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document specifically lays out the notification, many of the issues which we discussed yesterday. When one looks at the date of this document, looks at what happened in context afterwards, it's clear that just like other notifications, you know, at some point even the UN senior leadership became aware that the BiH was intending to break the cease-fire and to resume offensive activities. I think this document is a reflection of that, and given where this document -- who authored it and where it was sent to, it's fair to conclude that that notification went to the highest levels within the United Nations within the department of peacekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the documents that we saw yesterday about the activation of the armed forces in Zepa and Srebrenica, as a soldier would you consider it justifiable to take steps preparing for combat activities in the territory of an enclave where armed forces were not supposed to exist to begin with? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Justifiable in a sense of the Bosnian government's military objectives, yes. Justifiable in the sense of legal obligations in a cease-fire zone is a different question. As you noted, it was supposedly demilitarised; therefore, if they were properly demilitarised you wouldn't have the situation where in the enclaves those forces are mobilising and preparing for combat activities. As we know, that was not the case. So, again, since this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And was the least that the Army of Republika Srpska could do to prevent the army that UNPROFOR failed to disarm in the demilitarised zones of Zepa and Srebrenica from arming -- from arming -- to prevent them from arming through various restrictions. That's what should stand at the end of my question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now it's clear. Yes, sir, from a military perspective, the idea that the Army Republika Srpska would take steps to ensure that their adversary -- their armed adversary within the enclave was not surreptitiously receiving weapons is something that they would have been actively involved in and were actively involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the Army of Republika Srpska able to have any impact on the distribution of humanitarian aid in the enclaves and prevent the aid from being distributed to the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska was able to control the flow going into the enclaves by virtue of convoys and inspections. Once a convoy passed through that final check-point and went into the enclave, they obviously had no material ability to affect where in the enclave that material went and whom ultimately consumed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the army that had not been disarmed in the enclaves did require some sort of logistics, do you happen to know in what way the BH Army received food supplies and other logistical supplies in Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the pattern that has been established is quite clear. Those supplies that were overtly military, such as weapons, grenades, mine, ammunition, were smuggled in over land or, in select case, brought in by helicopter. Those items that were considered to be dual-use, that had both military and civilian applications, such as food, such as fuel, things of that nature, the military within the enclave was content to be able to appropriate from the general supplies that were going to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The supplies intended for the civilian population that you mentioned in your answer, did they come from the various humanitarian convoys arriving in the enclave, such as UNPROFOR and UNHCR convoys among others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably to a larger extent from UNHCR convoys, to a lesser extent the UNPROFOR, since it wasn't their specific mandate to provide food to the larger civilian populations. So that is why in the context of those convoys there was attention paid to the amount of materials going in to try and ensure that the amount of materials there were going in were suitable for the civilian population but would not be in such excess that it would be diverted to military use. These are the -- the attention being paid to it was by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we are at the end of our work-day, I would ask that 1D924 be admitted into evidence. That's the report by Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it there is no B/C/S translation. If you don't insist to receive a translation into B/C/S, it will be -- or, I should ask you if you want to have a translation. Have you contacted a translation unit? Mr. Gajic, what is your position? Otherwise we just receive it as a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the process is underway. The Case Manager is dealing with some issues, and I have taken on, myself, certain others, and I am sure that we will resolve the matter shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document -- I really didn't understand your response. Are you going to receive or request a translation or not? If you don't need a translation, it will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be good to have a translation because we find the document to be very important, and not just the portion shown to Mr. Butler. So we would be insisting on a translation. Can we have the document marked for identification until the translation is received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification pending translation, but it is your responsibility to make sure that a translation will be made.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 1D924 shall be assigned Exhibit D304 marked for identification pending B/C/S translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, and the Defence is aware of that obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of August, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
